Oncology is the branch of medicine concerned with the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. Mathematical models can be used to study how cancer develops, grows, and spreads. By providing quantitative and predictive frameworks, mathematical models allow hypotheses about cancer to be tested and evaluated. A carcinogen is any substance that causes cancer. Carcinogenesis is the process by which normal cells are transformed into cancer cells. A key observation that motivated many mathematical models of carcinogenesis is cancer incidence. Cancer incidence often increases rapidly with age, while the occurrence of cancer in an individual appears highly stochastic. However, patterns emerge when cancer incidence is examined across populations. These observations contributed to the development of multistage theories of carcinogenesis, which describe cancer development as a sequence of stages or changes in cells. Beginning in the 1920s, experiments involving chemical carcinogens provided evidence for the idea that cancer develops through multiple stages. In particular, applying two different carcinogens in sequence often produced higher cancer rates than applying a single carcinogen over time, leading to the two-stage model of carcinogenesis. Charles and Luce-Clausen developed one of the first quantitative multistage theories in the 1940s, using a mathematical model to describe the development of skin tumors in mice. Their work demonstrated how mathematical models could be used to connect assumptions about cellular changes with observed cancer incidence. Armitage and Doll further developed multistage theory in the 1950s, introducing more general mathematical models that allowed different rates for different stages and treated the stages as sequential cellular changes rather than necessarily genetic mutations. Their work helped establish mathematical modelling as a framework for studying the development of cancer. 2.3 What is a Mathematical Model? A mathematical model is a numerical representation of a real-world problem. By replacing physical experimentation with mathematical simulations, it allows researchers to evaluate system dynamics and predict future outcomes. 2.4 Systems of ODEs as Mathematical Models A system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) is a set of equations that involves two or more dependent variables that depend on one independent variable. A solution to this system is a set of functions that satisfies each equation on some interval \(I\). A system of ODEs can serve as a mathematical model by describing real world systems where multiple interacting components evolve over a shared independent variable. For example, in ecology, the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model uses a system of two coupled ODEs to track the interdependent population sizes of two interacting species over time \(t\). Many mathematical models are described using systems of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). It is useful to identify equilibrium points of a system of ODEs and study the stability of the equilibria. Consider the following system of ODEs: \[ rac{dx}{dt} = f(x,y)\] \[ rac{dy}{dt} = g(x,y)\] 2.5 Review of Mathematical Concepts 2.5.1 The Characteristic Equation For a square matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n 	imes n}\), the characteristic equation is given by \(\det(A - \lambda I) = 0\). This yields an \(n\)-degree polynomial whose roots correspond directly to the matrix’s eigenvalues \(\lambda\). 2.5.2 The Jacobian Matrix For a vector-valued function \(f: \mathbb{R}^n 	o \mathbb{R}^m\) given by \(f(x) = (f_1(x), \dots, f_m(x))\) where \(x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\), the Jacobian matrix \(J\) is the \(m 	imes n\) matrix of first-order partial derivatives: \[J =  egin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_n} \ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \ \dfrac{\partial f_m}{\partial x_1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial f_m}{\partial x_n} \end{pmatrix}\] When \(m=n\), i.e., the matrix is square, its determinant, commonly referred to as the Jacobian, acts as a local scaling factor. The Jacobian plays an essential role in coordinate transformations by describing how areas or volumes stretch, rotate, and distort under a change of variables. Consider the system of ODEs above. The Jacobian matrix of the system is \[J(x,y)=  egin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\ \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} \end{pmatrix}\] This matrix contains the first order partial derivatives of \(f\) and \(g\), describing how small changes in \(x\) and \(y\) affect the rate of change of the system. 2.5.3 Equilibrium Points and Local Stability An equilibrium point is a point \((x^*, y^*)\) such that \( rac{dx}{dt} = 0\) and \( rac{dy}{dt} = 0\). That is, an equilibrium point is a point at which both variables \(x\) and \(y\) remain constant over time. At an equilibrium, there is no net change in either variable. It is important to note that the equilibrium of a system does not mean that individual processes affecting \(x\) and \(y\) have stopped. Rather, the processes are balancing each other. Finding an equilibrium tells us where a system can remain unchanged, but does not tell us what happens if the system is slightly disturbed. Stability describes how a system behaves following a small deviation from an equilibrium. An equilibrium is stable if solutions that start sufficiently close to the equilibrium remain close to it. An equilibrium is asymptotically stable, if it is stable and solutions that start sufficiently close will eventually approach the equilibrium. An equilibrium is unstable if it is not stable. To study the local stability of an equilibrium \((x^*, y^*)\), we analyse the eigenvalues of \(J(x^*, y^*)\). Let \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) be eigenvalues of \(J(x^*, y^*)\), and \((x^*, y^*)\) an equilibrium point. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both real and negative, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is asymptotically stable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both real and positive, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is unstable. If \(\lambda _ 1 < 0\) and \(\lambda_2 > 0\), with both being real, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is called a saddle point and is unstable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both complex with negative real parts, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is asymptotically stable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both complex with positive real parts, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is unstable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both purely imaginary, then the linearized system exhibits oscillatory behaviour. Further analysis is required to determine stability. Zero eigenvalues require further analysis to determine stability. 2.6 Illustrative Example Consider the following model, describing a simple tumour-immune interaction based on the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey equations. Firstly, the activation term \(\alpha\) is simplistic and does not capture the complexities of immune responses to tumour growth. We also assumed proportional growth and decay, which is not realistic. Secondly, consider the case where there are no tumour cells (\(T=0\)). By (2.2), \( rac{dE}{dt}=-\delta E\). We get that \(E(t)= E(0)e^{-\delta t}\), implying that density of effector cells tends to zero over time. This is unrealistic, as effector cells are constantly present throughout the body. Thirdly, we are not modelling many factors that are involved in these tumour-effector cell interactions. This includes different tumour cell types, different effector cell types, and damage to healthy cells. Overall, this model simply demonstrates how a system of ordinary differential equations could be used to study tumour cell and effector cell interactions despite its limitations. Cancer cells grow and divide at a rapid pace, leading to the development of tumors. Early experimental studies on tumors study the rate of change of the volume, noticing that over time the growth rate decreased and necrotic cores could develop. Necrotic cores occur when cells at the middle of a tumor do not have enough nutrients and die en masse. Using a differential equation, we can model the tumor growth with regards to the nutrient density. 2.9.1 Modeling Assumptions The tumor stays a sphere and is axisymmetric The tumor not being axisymmetric would complicate the model by including terms dependent on angle, while not providing enough insight to justify the complication Nutrient is only consumed by living cells The system is at diffusive equilibrium, since nutrient diffusion happens in seconds but tumor growth happens over days If the system is not at diffusive equilibrium, we would have to model two timescales, this assumption simplifies the derivation Cancer cells die when the concentration of nutrient falls below a certain level Cells move towards the center as tumor grows 2.9.2 Parameters \(\sigma(r)\): nutrient concentration at radius point, \(r\) \(\hat{\sigma}\): nutrient concentration when slowed growth occurs \(\sigma_i\): critical nutrient concentration, ie \(\sigma<\sigma_i\) means that the cells dies \(\sigma_\infty\): constant nutrient concentration at surface, \(R_0\) \(A\): nutrient consumption, per unit time \(s\): proliferation, per unit time \(\lambda\): volume loss due to apoptosis, per unit time \(k\): diffusion constant \(R_0\): outer radius of tumor 2.9.3 Model Development The model has three separate growth regimes: fast growth, slow growth, and development of the necrotic core. Chapter 3 The Kuznetsov Tumour–Immune Model A tumour is an abnormal mass of tissue that forms when cells grow and divide more than they should or do not die when they should. Tumours may be benign (not cancer) or malignant (cancer). Malignant tumours can spread into, or invade, nearby tissues. They can also spread to other parts of the body through the blood and lymph systems. Tumour cells reproduce and therefore could increase the tumour population. Moreover, tumour cells can also be removed through interactions with immune effector cells. These cells recognize and respond to abnormal cells, including tumour cells. Some examples of these cells are cytotoxic T lymphocytes and natural killer cells. Define the following: \(E\): Number of effector cells located at the tumor site, \(T\): Number of tumor cells located at the tumor site, \(s\): Baseline rate at which mature effector cells enter the tumour region, \(p\): Rate of tumour stimulated effector cell accumulation \(g\): Saturation parameter for tumour stimulated effector cell accumulation, \(m\): Rate of effector cell inactivation due to interactions with tumour cells, \(n\): Rate of tumour cell killing through interactions with effector cells, \(d\): Rate of ordinary effector cell elimination \(a\): Maximum growth rate of the tumor cell population, \(b\): Inverse of maximum carrying capacity, where all of the above parameters are constant. To determine the rate of change of the effector cell population, we consider processes that increase and decrease the number of effector cells. Effector cells enter the tumour region at baseline rate \(s\). Tumour cells also stimulate the accumulation of effector cells. We assume that this stimulation increases with tumour cell number but eventually saturates, giving the term \( rac{pET}{g+T}\). The saturation reflects the assumption that the accumulation of effector cells cannot increase indefinitely as tumour size increases, due to biological limitations. Effector cells are also inactivated through interactions with tumour cells at a rate proportional to both \(E\) and \(T\), giving the term \(mET\). Finally, effector cells are eliminated naturally at a rate proportional to the size of the population, giving the term \(dE\). Combining these processes together, we obtain: \[ egin{equation}  rac{dE}{dt} = s +  rac{pET}{g+T} - mET -dE \label{eq:kuznetsov4a} \end{equation}\] Similarly, to determine the rate of change of the tumour cell population, we consider processes that increase and decrease the number of tumour cells. We assume that tumour cells undergo logistic growth. At low tumour cell numbers, growth is approximately exponential, while at high tumour cell numbers, growth slows due to limitations such as available resources. This gives the logistic growth term \(aT(1-bT)\). Tumour cells are also removed through interactions with immune effector cells. We assume that the rate of tumour cell killing is proportional to both the number of tumour cells and the number of effector cells, giving the term \(nET\). Combining tumour growth and immune mediated killing, we obtain: \[ egin{equation}  rac{dT}{dt} = aT(1-bT) -nET \label{eq:kuznetsov4b} \end{equation}\] Equations (ref?)(eq:kuznetsov4a) and (ref?)(eq:kuznetsov4b) form the reduced Kuznetsov tumour immune model. These equations form a system of ODEs describing the interactions between tumour cells and immune effector cells. 3.1 Analysing the Kuznetsov Model Recall that an equilibrium is a state where both \( rac{dE}{dt}=0\) and \( rac{dT}{dt}=0\). We first consider the case where there are no tumour cells, so \(T=0\). Equation (ref?)(eq:kuznetsov4a) becomes \[  rac{dE}{dt}=s-dE. \] Setting this equal to zero and solving for \(E\), we get \[ E= rac{s}{d}. \] Thus, the tumour free equilibrium is \[ (E_1,T_1)=( rac{s}{d},0). \] This equilibrium represents a state in which there are no tumour cells, while effector cells remain present due to the continuous baseline influx \(s\). We next consider equilibria where both \(T
eq0\) and \(E
eq0\). From equation (ref?)(eq:kuznetsov4b), setting \( rac{dT}{dt}=0\) gives \[ aT(1-bT)-nET=0. \] Factoring out \(T\) gives \[ T(a-abT-nE)=0. \] Since \(T
eq0\), we obtain \[ E= rac{a}{n}(1-bT). \] This is the tumour nullcline for positive tumour cell populations. Similarly, setting equation (ref?)(eq:kuznetsov4a) equal to zero gives \[ s+ rac{pET}{g+T}-mET-dE=0. \] Solving for \(E\), we get \[ E=  rac{s(g+T)} {d(g+T)+mT(g+T)-pT}. \] This is the effector cell nullcline. Therefore, positive equilibrium points occur at the intersections of the two nullclines. Depending on the parameter values, the model can have zero, one, two, or three positive equilibrium points. To analyse the stability around these equilibria, we first find the Jacobian matrix. Define \(f(E,T)= s+ rac{pET}{g+T}-mET-dE\) and \(g(E,T)= aT(1-bT)-nET\). The Jacobian matrix is \[ egin{pmatrix}  rac{pT}{g+T}-mT-d &  rac{pgE}{(g+T)^2}-mE \ -nT & a-2abT-nE \end{pmatrix}\] We first analyse the stability around the tumour free equilibrium. \[J(E_1,T_1)=  egin{pmatrix} -d &  rac{ps}{dg}-m rac{s}{d} \ 0 & a- rac{ns}{d} \end{pmatrix}\] The eigenvalues of \(J(E_1,T_1)\) are \(\lambda_1=-d\) and \(\lambda_2=a- rac{ns}{d}.\) Since \(d>0\), we always have \(\lambda_1<0\). The stability of the tumour free equilibrium therefore depends on the second eigenvalue. If \(a- rac{ns}{d}<0\), then both eigenvalues are negative and the tumour free equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable. If \(a- rac{ns}{d}>0\), the eigenvalues have opposite signs. Therefore, the tumour free equilibrium is a saddle point and is unstable. Notice that \(a\) represents the maximum tumour growth rate, while \( rac{ns}{d}\) represents the strength of tumour cell removal associated with the baseline effector population. Thus, the local stability of the tumour free state depends on the balance between tumour growth and immune mediated tumour removal. Kuznetsov et al. used experimental data from mice to obtain the following parameter values for the model. The parameters \(a\), \(b\), and \(s\) were specified based on experimental considerations, while the remaining parameters were estimated by nonlinear least-squares fitting.: \[ s=1.3	imes10^4,\quad p=0.1245,\quad g=2.019	imes10^7,\quad m=3.422	imes10^{-10}, \] \[ n=1.101	imes10^{-7},\quad d=0.0412,\quad a=0.18,\quad b=2.0	imes10^{-9}. \] using these, we get that the tumour free equilibrium is \((E_1,T_1)=( rac{s}{d},0)\approx(315534,0)\). Also, \(\lambda_1= -d = -0.0412\) and \(\lambda_2= a- rac{ns}{d} \approx 0.1453\). Since the eigenvalues have opposite signs, \((E_1,T_1)\) is a saddle point and is unstable. Now consider the case where \(E 
eq 0\) and \(T 
eq 0\). We will use the estimated parameter values to study stability in this case, since the equilibria depend on parameter values. Note that equilibria occur at the intersection of the tumour and effector cell nullclines. That is, they occur when \[  rac{a}{n}(1-bT) =  rac{s(g+T)} {d(g+T)+mT(g+T)-pT}. \] Using the estimated values, we get the following equilibria: \[ (E_2,T_2) = (1.608	imes10^6,\;8.186	imes10^6), \] \[ (E_3,T_3) = (7.585	imes10^5,\;2.680	imes10^8), \] and \[ (E_4,T_4) = (1.732	imes10^5,\;4.470	imes10^8). \] Now, we analyse the stability around each equilibrium. \[ J(E_2,T_2) \approx  egin{pmatrix} -0.00808 & 0.00447 \ -0.90132 & -0.00295 \end{pmatrix} \] has eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \approx -0.00552+0.06342i\) and \(\lambda_2 \approx -0.00552-0.06342i.\) Both eigenvalues are complex with negative real parts, thus the equilibrium \((E_2,T_2)\) is a stable focus. \[ J(E_3,T_3) \approx  egin{pmatrix} -0.01714 & -0.000237 \ -29.5093 & -0.09649 \end{pmatrix} \] has eigenvalues \(\lambda_1\approx0.03576\) and \(\lambda_2\approx-0.14936.\) Since the eigenvalues have opposite signs, \((E_3,T_3)\) is a saddle point and is unstable. \[ J(E_4,T_4) \approx  egin{pmatrix} -0.07505 & -0.0000573 \ -49.2175 & -0.16093 \end{pmatrix} \] has eigenvalues \(\lambda_1\approx-0.04970\) and \(\lambda_2\approx-0.18628.\) Since they are both negative, the \((E_4,T_4)\) is asymptotically stable. Department of Mathematics, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA 3.2 Coexistence equilibria: root structure and sign test A tumor-present equilibrium satisfies both nullclines of \(\eqref{eq:kuz_ODEs}\) simultaneously: \[ egin{equation} x = f(y) \equiv  rac{\sigma}{\delta+\mu y - \dfrac{ho y}{\eta+y}}, \qquad x = g(y) \equiv \alpha(1- eta y). \end{equation}\] Setting \(f(y)=g(y)\) and clearing the denominator \((\eta+y)\) yields a cubic polynomial in \(y\) (Kuznetsov et al.’s Equation 8): \[ egin{equation} C_3 y^3 + C_2 y^2 + C_1 y + C_0 = 0, \label{eq:kuz_cubic} \end{equation}\] with Each positive real root \(y^*\) of \(\eqref{eq:kuz_cubic}\) corresponds to a biologically admissible tumor-present equilibrium. Rather than solving the cubic directly, we can bound – and in this case pin down – the number of positive roots purely from the of its coefficients, using Descartes’ Rule of Signs: the number of positive real roots of a real polynomial is either equal to the number of sign changes in its ordered coefficient sequence, or less than that by an even number. Step 1: sign of \(C_3\). Since \(\mu, eta>0\), we always have \(C_3 = \mu eta>0\). Step 2: sign of \(C_0\). Directly from its definition, \(C_0>0 \iff \sigma/\alpha > \delta \iff \sigma/\delta > \alpha\) – exactly the tumor-free stability condition of Proposition \(ef{prop_kuz_tumorfree}\). So \(C_0<0\) precisely when the tumor-free state is unstable, which is the regime of interest, since it is the regime in which a tumor-present equilibrium must exist (by the Intermediate Value Theorem: the cubic \(F(y) = C_3y^3+C_2y^2+C_1y+C_0\) satisfies \(F(0)=C_0<0\) and \(F(y)	o+\infty\) as \(y	o\infty\), so it has at least one positive root). Step 3: sign of \(C_2\). Suppose effector activation dominates exhaustion in the sense that \(ho > \mu\eta+\delta\) – this holds for the fitted parameters in Table \(ef{tbl:kuz_param}\) and is a standing assumption in . Then \(\mu\eta+\delta-ho<0\), so \(C_2 = -\mu + (\mu\eta+\delta-ho) eta\) is the sum of two negative terms: \(C_2<0\) for every \( eta>0\). Step 4: sign of \(C_1\). Under the same condition \(ho>\mu\eta+\delta\), and since \(\sigma/\alpha>0\) and \(\delta\eta eta>0\), \[ C_1 =  rac{\sigma}{\alpha} + \underbrace{(ho-\mu\eta-\delta)}_{>0} + \delta\eta eta > 0. \] Putting it together. With \(C_0<0\), \(C_1>0\), \(C_2<0\), \(C_3>0\), the ordered coefficient sequence is \((+,-,+,-)\) (reading from \(C_3\) down to \(C_0\)), which has three sign changes. By Descartes’ Rule, the cubic \(\eqref{eq:kuz_cubic}\) therefore has either three or one positive real roots. Since we have already shown (Step 2) that at least one positive root always exists in this regime, and since three is the generic, structurally stable count predicted by the sign pattern, the system typically admits coexistence equilibria – producing, together with the unstable tumor-free state, a total of four steady states and the characteristic bistable “dormant tumor” / “tumor escape” structure that is the central result of . Descartes’ Rule alone cannot distinguish the three-root case from the (non-generic) one-root case within this sign pattern; a finer tool, a Sturm sequence built from \(C_0,C_1,C_2\) and the auxiliary quantities \(S=C_2C_1-9C_3C_0\), \(T=2C_2S/R-3C_3S^2/R^2-C_1\), and \(R=2C_2^2-6C_3C_1\), is needed to certify the exact count in borderline cases; see for the full Sturm-sequence table. Checking the fitted parameters. Using the values in Table \(ef{tbl:kuz_param}\): \(\mu\eta+\delta = (0.00311)(20.19)+0.3743 \approx 0.437\), which is indeed less than \(ho=1.131\), confirming Steps 3–4. And \(\sigma/\delta = 0.1181/0.3743 \approx 0.316\), which is less than \(\alpha=1.636\), confirming the tumor-free state is unstable (Step 2). The sign sequence is therefore \((+,-,+,-)\) as derived above, correctly predicting the three coexistence equilibria – the “dormant tumor” state, a saddle, and the “tumor escape” state – that finds numerically and uses to build their bifurcation diagram and phase portrait.

Chapter 4 Extending the Model: An Immune-Resistant Tumor Subpopulation 4.1 Motivation and model equations 4.2 Mechanistic derivation of \(\theta\), \(\rho_T\), and \(\mu_T\) 4.3 Equilibria and stability 4.4 Root structure and sign test

Chapter 4 Extending the Model: An Immune-Resistant Tumor Subpopulation 4.1 Motivation and model equations The Kuznetsov model of Section \(\ref{sec:kuznetsov}\) treats the tumor as a single, immunologically uniform population. Real tumors, however, are heterogeneous, and subclones that partially evade immune-mediated killing are a central driver of treatment failure. As a first extension, we equip the tumor cell population \(T\) with a degree of immune resistance, benchmarked directly against the Kuznetsov model so that setting the resistance parameters to their “no resistance” values recovers Section \(\ref{sec:kuznetsov}\) exactly. The model presented here is the single-subpopulation special case of a more general two-subpopulation (immune-resistant vs. immune-sensitive, with optional chemotherapy resistance) model developed in , to which we refer the reader for the full treatment, including both immune-evasion mechanisms considered simultaneously with chemotherapy. We assume resistance carries a growth-rate cost \(\zeta>0\), so the resistant population’s growth rate is \(\alpha_T=\alpha-\zeta\) rather than the wild-type rate \(\alpha\), and confers a benefit \(\theta\in[0,1]\) that reduces the effectiveness of effector-mediated killing (\(\theta=1\) recovers full susceptibility, i.e. no resistance). Writing \(E\) for the effector population and \(\kappa=1/\beta\) for the carrying capacity, the dynamics are This is structurally identical to \(\eqref{eq:kuz_ODEs}\): tumor growth is logistic and suppressed by effector-mediated killing at rate \(\theta E\); effectors are produced at baseline rate \(\sigma\), activated through a saturating term with parameters \(\rho_T,\eta\), exhausted or inactivated by the tumor at rate \(\mu_T\), and die naturally at rate \(\delta\). The only change is that the activation and inactivation parameters, \(\rho_T\) and \(\mu_T\), and the effective growth rate \(\alpha_T\) and kill-rate reduction \(\theta\), now depend on the resistance mechanism the tumor employs, as derived mechanistically below. Setting \(\theta=1\), \(\alpha_T=\alpha\), \(\rho_T=\rho\), \(\mu_T=\mu\) recovers \(\eqref{eq:kuz_ODEs}\) exactly, confirming this is a proper extension rather than a different model. 4.2 Mechanistic derivation of \(\theta\), \(\rho_T\), and \(\mu_T\) As in the Kuznetsov model, effectors and tumor cells transiently bind to form a conjugate \(C\), which then dissociates leaving either cell undamaged, the tumor cell lethally hit, or the effector cell inactivated (Figure \(\ref{fig:red_ET_diagram}\)). Immune resistance is modeled as a change in the rates governing this reaction scheme relative to a wild-type (non-resistant) baseline, denoted with a superscript \((0)\). Assuming the conjugate dynamics equilibrate on a fast time scale relative to cell division and death (the same quasi-steady-state argument used in to derive \(\eqref{eq:kuz_ODEs}\) from the underlying reaction scheme), we have \(C = \Gamma E T\) with \(\Gamma = \gamma_1/(\gamma_{-1}+\gamma_2+\gamma_3)\). After rescaling by the wild-type reference rate \(\gamma_2^{(0)}\Gamma^{(0)}\), the reduced system \(\eqref{eq:red_ODEs}\) follows with \[\begin{equation} \theta = \frac{\gamma_2\Gamma}{\gamma_2^{(0)}\Gamma^{(0)}}, \qquad \rho_T=\rho\,\frac{\Gamma}{\Gamma^{(0)}}, \qquad \mu_T = \frac{\gamma_3\Gamma}{\gamma_2^{(0)}\Gamma^{(0)}}. \end{equation}\] We consider two concrete resistance mechanisms: The distinction between the two mechanisms is therefore whether resistance acts on the of an effector–tumor encounter (checkpoint evasion) or on the of encounter itself (reduced antigen presentation). Table \(\ref{tbl:red_param}\) summarizes the parameters of the extended model, reusing the Kuznetsov baseline values from Table \(\ref{tbl:kuz_param}\) for all quantities unrelated to resistance. 4.3 Equilibria and stability The system \(\eqref{eq:red_ODEs}\) admits a tumor-free equilibrium \(\mathcal{E}_0 = (0, \sigma/\delta)\) – identical in form to the Kuznetsov tumor-free state, since resistance only affects the dynamics once \(T>0\) – and, when it exists, a tumor-present equilibrium \(\mathcal{E}_1=(T^*,E^*)\) with \(T^*>0\). Exactly as in Section \(\ref{sec:kuznetsov}\), the Jacobian at \(\mathcal{E}_0\) is triangular, with eigenvalues \[\begin{equation} \lambda_1 = \alpha_T - \theta\,\frac{\sigma}{\delta}, \qquad \lambda_2 = -\delta, \end{equation}\] giving the following direct generalization of Proposition \(\ref{prop_kuz_tumorfree}\). At a tumor-present equilibrium, \(T^*\) and \(E^*\) satisfy \[\begin{equation} E^* = \alpha_T\left(1-\frac{T^*}{\kappa}\right) = \frac{\sigma}{\dfrac{\rho_T T^*}{T^*+\eta} - \mu_T T^* - \delta}. \label{eq:red_eq_condition} \end{equation}\] 4.4 Root structure and sign test Clearing denominators in Equation \(\eqref{eq:red_eq_condition}\), exactly as was done for the Kuznetsov model in Section \(\ref{sec:kuznetsov}\), gives the cubic polynomial \[\begin{equation} F(T^*) = B_3 T^{*3} + B_2 T^{*2} + B_1 T^* + B_0 = 0, \label{eq:red_cubic} \end{equation}\] with coefficients One can check directly that \(B_i = \alpha_T\kappa\,C_i'\) for \(i=0,\dots,3\), where \(C_i'\) denotes the Kuznetsov coefficient \(C_i\) of Section \(\ref{sec:kuznetsov}\) with \((\alpha,\rho,\mu,\beta)\) replaced by \((\alpha_T,\rho_T,\mu_T,1/\kappa)\). Since multiplying a polynomial by the positive constant \(\alpha_T\kappa\) does not change its roots, \(\eqref{eq:red_cubic}\) has exactly the same positive-root structure as the Kuznetsov cubic with resistant parameters substituted in – confirming that resistance enters the equilibrium problem only by remapping the same three parameters that already governed the wild-type dynamics. The same four-step sign test from Section \(\ref{sec:kuznetsov}\) therefore applies verbatim: As before, the sign sequence \((+,-,+,-)\) has three sign changes, so Descartes’ Rule predicts either one or three positive roots of \(\eqref{eq:red_cubic}\), with three being the generic case – the hallmark of bistability between a low- and a high-tumor-burden resistant equilibrium. This is exactly the qualitative structure established for the Kuznetsov model in Section \(\ref{sec:kuznetsov}\), now shown to persist under both forms of immune resistance considered here, provided effector activation continues to dominate tumor-induced exhaustion (\(\rho_T>\mu_T\eta+\delta\)) at the resistant phenotype’s parameter values. The Jacobian at \(\mathcal{E}_1\) is \[\begin{equation} J(\mathcal{E}_1) = \begin{pmatrix} -\dfrac{\alpha_T}{\kappa}T^* & -\theta T^* \\[8pt] E^*\left(\dfrac{\rho_T\eta}{(T^*+\eta)^2} - \mu_T\right) & -\dfrac{\sigma}{E^*} \end{pmatrix}, \end{equation}\] with \(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(J(\mathcal{E}_1))<0\) and \[\begin{equation} \det(J(\mathcal{E}_1)) = \frac{\alpha_T\sigma}{\kappa E^*}T^* + \left(\frac{\rho_T\eta}{(T^*+\eta)^2}-\mu_T\right)\theta E^* T^*. \end{equation}\] As in the wild-type model, \(\mathcal{E}_1\) is stable whenever \(\det(J(\mathcal{E}_1))>0\), which holds in particular if \(\rho_T\eta/(T^*+\eta)^2 > \mu_T\); otherwise, bistability between a low- and high-tumor-burden resistant equilibrium arises via the usual saddle-node bifurcation structure, consistent with the three-root sign-test result above.

Chapter 5 Summary Starting from the two-population Kuznetsov tumor–immune model, we showed that its coexistence-equilibrium structure is governed by a cubic polynomial whose coefficient signs – not its explicit roots – determine whether the system is monostable or bistable. The same sign-test machinery, applied unchanged after remapping three parameters to account for a resistant phenotype, shows that an immune-resistant tumor subpopulation inherits the same qualitative bistability whenever effector activation continues to dominate tumor-induced exhaustion at the resistant phenotype’s parameter values. This worked example illustrates a general strategy for analyzing tumor–immune models in this course: reduce the equilibrium condition to a low-degree polynomial, and use a sign test on its coefficients, rather than brute-force root-finding, to characterize the number and type of biologically admissible steady states. % %

Chapter 6 Agent-Based Modeling 6.1 Chapter Overview and Learning Objectives 6.1.1 Learning Objectives (To be developed by Maria) 6.1.2 Prerequisites and Recommended Background (To be developed by Maria) 6.2 Introduction: Why Agent-Based Modeling in Oncology? 6.2.1 Comparing Modeling Approaches: ODEs vs. ABMs (To be developed by Maria) 6.2.2 When to Use ABMs in Cancer Biology (To be developed by Maria) 6.3 The Four Pillar Ingredients of an Oncology ABM Ordinary differential equation (ODE) models treat populations as continuous averages. In reality, however, cancer is driven by three factors: individual differences between cells, competition for space, and direct interactions with their surroundings. To capture these biological dynamics in a computer simulation, Agent-Based Models (ABMs) rely on four core building blocks: 6.3.1 Agents and State Variables Agents are independent computational entities representing individual biological actors (for example, tumor cells, cytotoxic T lymphocytes, macrophages, or stromal fibroblasts). Each agent maintains its own internal state variables, which may include: Spatial Coordinates: Position \((x, y)\) on a discrete lattice or continuous coordinate space. Agent Type / Phenotype: Cell lineage (e.g., prey/tumor cell vs. predator/immune cell, stem-like vs. differentiated, sensitive vs. drug-resistant). Internal Resources / Health: Energy level, cell volume, or damage accumulation (e.g., DNA double-strand breaks). Lifecycle Status: Active/proliferating, quiescent, senescent, or flagged for death (apoptotic/necrotic). 6.3.2 Environment (The World) The environment represents the physical tissue domain and biochemical landscape in which agents live: Spatial Topology: Typically presented as a 2D or 3D grid. The boundaries can be reflective (rigid walls) or periodic (wrapping around edges so cells exiting the right re-enter on the left). Physical Exclusion: Rules dictating whether a single lattice site can host multiple agents or enforces volume control (carrying capacity per cell). Background resources: Gradients of extracellular nutrients (glucose, oxygen), chemokines, or therapeutic drugs that diffuse, decay, and are consumed by agents. 6.3.3 Interaction and Behavior Rules Rules define how each cell behaves and makes decisions at every step of the simulation. Some examples include: Movement: Random walks, contact-inhibited crawling, or chemotaxis toward nutrient sources. Feeding & Metabolism: Extracting energy from the local environment or prey to fuel baseline basal metabolic costs. Immune Attacks (Predation): Immune cells spotting cancer cells upon physical proximity, causing them to lock onto them and destroy them (cell lysis). Reproduction (Proliferation): Dividing into daughter cells when internal energy exceeds a threshold and space is available. Cell Death (Apoptosis): Cell death triggered by starvation (energy dropping below zero), immune destruction, or senescence. 6.3.4 Iterative Scheduling Loop Time advances in discrete increments (\(\Delta t\)). At each time step: Activation Order: Living agents are activated. In asynchronous scheduling, the order is randomized at every step to prevent execution order artifacts. Action Execution: Each agent evaluates its local neighborhood, updates its energy, moves, interacts, and potentially reproduces or dies. Environmental Update: Diffusive fields diffuse/decay and renewable resources regenerate. State Census: Macroscopic summary statistics (e.g., total population counts, spatial clustering) are logged for analysis. 6.4 Hands-On Implementation Walkthrough: Predator-Prey in R & Plotly Recall that in Chapter 1, we introduced the continuous Lotka-Volterra system to model the high level interaction between immune effector cells (\(E\), predators) and tumour cells (\(T\), prey): \[\frac{dT}{dt} = a T - b T E, \quad \frac{dE}{dt} = c T E - d E\] While ODEs predict deterministic oscillations, real biological microenvironments display uneven spatial distribution, random local die-offs, and localized cell clustering. Here, we build an agent-based counterpart in R, using Plotly to visualize both the spatial grid and macroscopic population curves. Two Ways to Run and Interact with this Model Option 1: In-Browser Exploration How to interact: Hover: Hover your mouse over any cell or agent to view its exact \((x, y)\) coordinates and internal energy level. Zoom & Pan: Click and drag a box across the grid to zoom into localized cell clusters; double-click to reset the view. Filter Traces: Click individual labels in the legend (e.g., Prey, Predators, Grass) to hide or isolate specific populations. Option 2: Shiny Application A shiny application is a standalone interactive application featuring real-time animation, step-by-step playback, and dynamic parameter sweeps. How to run: Ensure shiny and plotly are installed (install.packages(c("shiny", "plotly"))). Open scripts/predator_prey_app.R in RStudio and click the green “Run App” button at the top right of the editor, or run shiny::runApp("scripts/predator_prey_app.R") in the R console. How to interact: Adjust parameter sliders for initial cell counts, grid dimensions, and reproduction probabilities. Click Play / Pause or Step once to watch predator-prey hunting, reproduction, and nutrient regrowth unfold in real time. Switch presets between Stable Coexistence and Default (Predator Extinction) to observe system bifurcation. 6.4.1 Model Formulation and Parameters Our spatial ecosystem consists of: Prey (Tumor / Sheep): Move into unoccupied neighboring patches, consume background resources (grass/nutrients), expend energy to survive, and divide upon acquiring sufficient energy. Predators (Immune / Wolves): Actively search for prey, consume prey on the same lattice site, gain energy from predation, and divide probabilistically. Renewable Resource Field (Nutrients / Grass): Spatial patches that regenerate after a fixed countdown period once consumed. m$energy[i] - 1 if (m$energy[i] < 0) { kill_agent(m, i) return(invisible()) } # Feeding if (t == SHEEP) { if (m$fully[m$x[i], m$y[i]]) { m$energy[i] <- m$energy[i] + m$de[SHEEP] m$fully[m$x[i], m$y[i]] <- FALSE } } else { dinner <- which(m$alive & m$type == SHEEP & m$x == m$x[i] & m$y == m$y[i]) if (length(dinner) > 0) { kill_agent(m, dinner[1]) m$energy[i] <- m$energy[i] + m$de[WOLF] } } # Reproduction if (runif(1) <= m$rp[t]) reproduce(m, i) } 6.4.3.3 Environmental Regeneration and Model Step Loop grass_step <- function(m) { growing <- !m$fully ready <- growing & m$countdown <= 0 m$fully[ready] <- TRUE m$countdown[ready] <- m$regrowth dec <- growing & !ready m$countdown[dec] <- m$countdown[dec] - 1L } model_step <- function(m) { # Asynchronous random scheduling: shuffle living agent indices ids <- which(m$alive) ids <- ids[sample.int(length(ids))] for (i in ids) if (m$alive[i]) agent_step(m, i) grass_step(m) m$step <- m$step + 1L m$h_step <- c(m$h_step, m$step) m$h_sheep <- c(m$h_sheep, sum(m$alive & m$type == SHEEP)) m$h_wolf <- c(m$h_wolf, sum(m$alive & m$type == WOLF)) m$h_grass <- c(m$h_grass, sum(m$fully)) # Occasionally drop dead agents so vectors do not grow without bound if (length(m$alive) > 4 * sum(m$alive) + 500) { keep <- m$alive m$type <- m$type[keep] m$x <- m$x[keep] m$y <- m$y[keep] m$energy <- m$energy[keep] m$alive <- m$alive[keep] } } 6.4.4
